shared_turn_1.user_message: How does a government knows the exact amount of physical money at any point in circulation?!
shared_turn_1.assistant_response:
Governments track physical currency through their central banks, which act as the sole issuers. Every banknote has a unique serial number recorded during production. When cash is printed, it enters the "currency in circulation" ledger.

Banks and businesses deposit excess cash back into the central bank or commercial banking system. The central bank counts these deposits and removes worn-out notes from circulation. By subtracting the amount held by banks (vault cash) from the total issued, they calculate the exact figure of money physically held by the public. This real-time accounting ensures precise tracking of every bill's status, whether it is in a vault or in someone's pocket.
